'''Daniel Julius Bernstein''' (born October 29, 1971) is an American [[mathematician]], [[cryptologist]], and [[computer scientist]]. He is a [[professor]] of computer science at the [[University of Illinois Chicago]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bernstein |first1=Daniel |title=Positions |url=https://cr.yp.to/positions.html |website=cr.yp.to |access-date=26 May 2025}}</ref> He was a visiting professor in the department of mathematics and computer science at the [[Eindhoven University of Technology]],<ref>{{cite web | title=Ruhr University Bochum and other places | website=ResearchGate | date=2023-12-08 | url=https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/Daniel-J-Bernstein-69944562 | access-date=2024-12-09}}</ref> and a [[visiting professor]] at CASA at [[Ruhr University Bochum]] through 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-12-18 |title=CASA team |url=https://casa.rub.de/ueber-casa/team |access-date=2024-11-16 |archive-date=2023-12-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231218203136/https://casa.rub.de/ueber-casa/team |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref>

== Early life ==
Bernstein attended [[Bellport High School]], a public high school on [[Long Island]], graduating in 1987 at the age of 15.<ref>{{cite news | date = 1987-01-21 | newspaper = New York Times | title = New Yorkers Excel In Contest | url = https://www.nytimes.com/1987/01/21/nyregion/new-yorkers-excel-in-contest.html | access-date= November 9, 2008 }}</ref> The same year, he ranked fifth in the [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]].<ref>{{cite news | date = 1987-01-21 | newspaper = New York Times | title = TWO GIRLS WIN WESTINGHOUSE COMPETITION | url = https://www.nytimes.com/1987/03/03/science/two-girls-win-westinghouse-competition.html | access-date= March 14, 2011 }}</ref> In 1987, he achieved a Top 10 ranking in the [[William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition]],<ref>{{cite news|jstor=2322251|title=The William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition|date=Oct 1988 |pages=717–727|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|author1=L. F. Klosinski|author2=G. L. Alexanderson|author2-link=Gerald L. Alexanderson|author3= L. C. Larson|volume=95|issue=8}}</ref> and was a member of the second-place team from [[Princeton University]] the following year.<ref>{{cite news|jstor=2324716|title=The William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition|date=Oct 1989|pages=688–695|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|author1=L. F. Klosinski|author2=G. L. Alexanderson|author2-link=Gerald L. Alexanderson|author3= L. C. Larson|volume=96|issue=8}}</ref> Bernstein earned a B.A. in mathematics from [[New York University]] (1991) and a Ph.D. in mathematics from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] (1995), where he studied under [[Hendrik Lenstra]].<ref name="cv" />

== ''Bernstein v. United States'' ==
{{Main|Bernstein v. United States}}

The [[export of cryptography from the United States]] was controlled as a [[munition]] starting from the [[Cold War]] until recategorization in 1996, with further relaxation in the late 1990s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://users.ece.cmu.edu/~adrian/630-f04/readings/crypto-law-survey2.html|title=Crypto Law Survey - Overview per country|last=Koops|first=Bert-Jaap|date=August 2004|website=Bert-Jaap Koops homepage|access-date=2019-03-21}}</ref> In 1995, Bernstein brought the court case ''[[Bernstein v. United States]]''. The ruling in the case declared that software was [[protected speech]] under the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]], which contributed to regulatory changes reducing controls on encryption.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2015/04/remembering-case-established-code-speech|title=EFF at 25: Remembering the Case that Established Code as Speech|last=Dame-Boyle|first=Alison|date=2015-04-16|website=Electronic Frontier Foundation|language=en|access-date=2019-03-21}}</ref> Bernstein was originally represented by the [[Electronic Frontier Foundation]].<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.com/1996/06/esbernstein/|title=Reluctant Hero|last=Cassidy|first=Peter|date=1996-06-01|magazine=Wired|access-date=2019-03-21|issn=1059-1028}}</ref> He later [[Pro se legal representation in the United States|represented himself]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cr.yp.to/export/2002/08.02-bernstein-subst.pdf|title=Plaintiff's Notice Of Substitution of Counsel|date=2002-10-07|access-date=2019-03-20}}</ref>

== Cryptography ==
Bernstein designed the [[Salsa20]] [[stream cipher]] in 2005 and submitted it to [[eSTREAM]] for review and possible standardization. He later published the [[ChaCha20]] variant of Salsa in 2008. In 2005, he proposed the [[Elliptic-curve cryptography|elliptic curve]] [[Curve25519]] as a basis for [[public-key cryptography|public-key]] schemes.  He worked as the lead researcher on the [[Ed25519]] version of [[EdDSA]]. The algorithms made their way into popular software. For example, since 2014, when [[OpenSSH]] is compiled without [[OpenSSL]], they power most of its operations. [[OpenBSD]] package [[Digital signature|signing]] is based on Ed25519.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://it.slashdot.org/story/14/04/30/1822209/openssh-no-longer-has-to-depend-on-openssl |title= OpenSSH No Longer Has To Depend On OpenSSL |first=Constantine A. |last=Murenin |editor=Soulskill |date=2014-04-30 |access-date=2014-12-26 |publisher=[[Slashdot]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://bsd.slashdot.org/story/14/01/19/0124202/openbsd-moving-towards-signed-packages-based-on-d-j-bernstein-crypto |title= OpenBSD Moving Towards Signed Packages — Based On D. J. Bernstein Crypto |first=Constantine A. |last=Murenin |editor=Soulskill |date=2014-01-19 |access-date=2014-12-27 |publisher=[[Slashdot]]}}</ref>

Nearly a decade later, [[Edward Snowden]] [[Global surveillance disclosures (2013–present)|disclosed mass surveillance]] by the [[National Security Agency]], and researchers discovered a [[Backdoor (computing)|backdoor]] in the Agency's [[Dual EC DRBG]] algorithm. These events raised suspicions of the elliptic curve parameters proposed by NSA and standardized by [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|NIST]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://safecurves.cr.yp.to/|title=SafeCurves: choosing safe curves for elliptic-curve cryptography|last1=Bernstein|first1=Daniel J.|last2=Lange|first2=Tanja|date=2017-01-22|access-date=2019-03-20}}</ref> Many researchers feared<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://lists.torproject.org/pipermail/tor-talk/2013-September/029956.html|title=[tor-talk] NIST approved crypto in Tor?|last=Maxwell|first=Gregory|date=September 8, 2013|access-date=2015-05-20}}</ref> that the NSA had chosen curves that gave them a [[Cryptanalysis|cryptanalytic]] advantage.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://safecurves.cr.yp.to/rigid.html|title=SafeCurves: Rigidity|website=safecurves.cr.yp.to|access-date=2015-05-20}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2013/09/the_nsa_is_brea.html#c1675929|title=The NSA Is Breaking Most Encryption on the Internet - Schneier on Security|website=www.schneier.com|date=5 September 2013 |access-date=2015-05-20}}</ref> [[Google]] selected ChaCha20 along with Bernstein's [[Poly1305]] [[message authentication code]] for use in [[Transport Layer Security|TLS]], which is widely used for Internet security.<ref name="chacha20poly1305">{{cite news|url=https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-tls-chacha20-poly1305-04|title=ChaCha20-Poly1305 Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS) |author=A. Langley |author2=W. Chang |author3=N. Mavrogiannopoulos |author4=J. Strombergson |author5=S. Josefsson|date=2015-12-16|work=[[Internet Draft]]}}</ref> Many protocols based on his works have been adopted by various [[Standards organization|standards organizations]] and are [[Curve25519#Applications|used in a variety of applications]], such as [[Apple iOS]],<ref>[https://www.apple.com/business/docs/iOS_Security_Guide.pdf iOS Security Guide]</ref> the [[Linux]] kernel,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://lwn.net/Articles/686033/|title=Replacing /dev/urandom|author=Corbet, Jonathan|website=Linux Weekly News|access-date=2016-09-20}}
</ref> [[OpenSSH]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://bxr.su/OpenBSD/usr.bin/ssh/PROTOCOL.chacha20poly1305|title=ssh/PROTOCOL.chacha20poly1305|last=Miller|first=Damien|date=2016-05-03|website=Super User's BSD Cross Reference: PROTOCOL.chacha20poly1305|access-date=2016-09-07}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://it.slashdot.org/story/13/12/11/173213/openssh-has-a-new-cipher-chacha20-poly1305-from-dj-bernstein|title=OpenSSH Has a New Cipher — Chacha20-poly1305 — from D.J. Bernstein|last=Murenin|first=Constantine A.|date=2013-12-11|editor=Unknown Lamer|publisher=[[Slashdot]]|access-date=2016-09-07}}</ref> and [[Tor (anonymity network)|Tor]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://gitweb.torproject.org/torspec.git/tree/tor-spec.txt?id=b5b771b19df9fc052b424228045409467a7b6414#n81|title=Tor's Protocol Specifications - Blog|author=Roger Dingledine & Nick Mathewson|access-date=20 December 2014}}</ref>

In spring 2005, Bernstein taught a course on "high speed cryptography."<ref>{{cite web | url = https://cr.yp.to/2005-590.html | author= Daniel J. Bernstein | title= MCS 590, High-Speed Cryptography, Spring 2005 | work= Authenticators and signatures | access-date= September 23, 2005 }}</ref> He introduced new [[Side-channel attacks|cache attacks]] against implementations of [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]] in the same time period.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://cr.yp.to/antiforgery/cachetiming-20050414.pdf | author = Daniel J. Bernstein | title = Cache timing attacks on AES |website=cr.yp.to | date = 2004-04-17}}</ref>

In April 2008,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ecrypt.eu.org/stream/portfolio.pdf |author1=Steve Babbage |author2=Christophe De Canniere |author3=Anne Canteaut |author3-link=Anne Canteaut |author4=Carlos Cid |author5=Henri Gilbert |author6=Thomas Johansson |author7=Matthew Parker |author8=Bart Preneel |author9=Vincent Rijmen |author10=Matthew Robshaw |title=The eSTREAM Portfolio |access-date=April 28, 2010 |archive-date=August 13, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120813112048/http://www.ecrypt.eu.org/stream/portfolio.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Bernstein's [[stream cipher]] "[[Salsa20]]" was selected as a member of the final portfolio of the [[eSTREAM]] project, part of a [[European Union]] research directive.

In 2011, Bernstein published RFSB, a variant of the [[fast syndrome-based hash|fast syndrome-based (FSB) hash]] function.

He is one of the editors of the 2009 book ''Post-Quantum Cryptography''.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.springer.com/us/book/9783540887010|title=Post-Quantum Cryptography|date=2009|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-3-540-88701-0|editor-last=Bernstein|editor-first=Daniel J.|location=Berlin Heidelberg|doi=10.1007/978-3-540-88702-7|s2cid=24166515 |language=en|editor-last2=Buchmann|editor-first2=Johannes|editor-last3=Dahmen|editor-first3=Erik}}</ref>

In 2022, Bernstein filed a second lawsuit against the U.S. government under the [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|Freedom of Information Act]], seeking records on the National Security Agency's role in influencing NIST's [[post-quantum cryptography]] standards, a case that remains ongoing as of 2025.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://blog.cr.yp.to/20220805-nsa.html|title=NSA, NIST, and post-quantum cryptography|last=Bernstein|first=Daniel J.|date=August 5, 2022|website=The cr.yp.to blog|access-date=November 24, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://nist.pqcrypto.org/foia/index.html|title=NSA-NIST-PQC FOIA responses|last=Bernstein|first=Daniel J.|date=2025|website=Post-quantum cryptography|access-date=November 24, 2025}}</ref>

== Software ==
Starting in the mid-1990s, Bernstein wrote a number of security-aware programs, including [[qmail]], [[ezmlm]], [[djbdns]], [[ucspi-tcp]], [[daemontools]], and <code>publicfile</code>.

Bernstein criticized the leading [[Domain Name System|DNS]] package at the time, [[BIND]], and wrote djbdns as a DNS package with security as a primary goal.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=F1FquvLFolIC&pg=PT190|title=Linux Server Security|last=Bauer|first=Michael D.|date=2005|publisher=O'Reilly Media, Inc.|isbn=978-0-596-00670-9|pages=172–173|language=en}}</ref> Bernstein offers "security guarantees" for qmail and djbdns in the form of monetary rewards for the identification of flaws.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ksqi5sl_JugC&pg=PA769|title=Ubuntu Linux Bible|last=Hagen|first=William von|date=2007-03-26|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-0-470-12454-3|page=769|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.admin-magazine.com/Articles/TinyDNS|title=Lighten Your DNS Load with TinyDNS|last=Binnie|first=Chris|website=ADMIN Magazine|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-21}}</ref> A purported exploit targeting qmail running on [[64-bit computing|64-bit platforms]] was published in 2005,<ref>{{cite web| author = Georgi Guninski| date = 2005-05-31| title = Georgi Guninski security advisory #74, 2005| url = https://www.guninski.com/where_do_you_want_billg_to_go_today_4.html| access-date= September 23, 2005 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web| author = James Craig Burley| date = 2005-05-31| title = My Take on Georgi Guninski's qmail Security Advisories| url = http://www.jcb-sc.com/qmail/guninski.html| access-date = 2007-08-24| archive-date = 2007-08-25| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070825110407/http://www.jcb-sc.com/qmail/guninski.html| url-status = dead}}</ref> but Bernstein believes that the exploit does not fall within the parameters of his qmail security guarantee. In March 2009, Bernstein awarded $1000 to Matthew Dempsky for finding a security flaw in [[djbdns]].<ref>{{cite web | author = Daniel J. Bernstein | date = 2009-03-04 | title = djbdns<=1.05 lets AXFRed subdomains overwrite domains | url = https://article.gmane.org/gmane.network.djbdns/13864 | access-date = 2009-03-04 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090305125545/http://article.gmane.org/gmane.network.djbdns/13864 | archive-date = 2009-03-05 }}</ref>

In August 2008, Bernstein announced<ref>{{cite web| author = Daniel J. Bernstein | title = High-speed cryptography| url = https://marc.info/?l=djbdns&m=122011940521548&w=2}}</ref> [[DNSCurve]], a proposal to secure the [[Domain Name System]]. DNSCurve applies techniques from [[elliptic curve cryptography]] with the goal of providing a vast increase in performance over the [[RSA (algorithm)|RSA]] public-key algorithm used by [[DNSSEC]]. It uses the existing DNS hierarchy to propagate trust by embedding public keys into specially formatted, [[Backward compatibility|backward-compatible]] DNS records.

Bernstein proposed [[Internet Mail 2000]], an alternative system for electronic mail, which he intended to replace the [[Simple Mail Transfer Protocol]] (SMTP), the [[Post Office Protocol]] (POP3) and the [[Internet Message Access Protocol]] (IMAP).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Internet Mail 2000 |url=https://cr.yp.to/im2000.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230125001404/https://cr.yp.to/im2000.html |archive-date=25 January 2023 |access-date=13 March 2023 |website=cr.yp.to}}</ref>

Bernstein is also known for his [[Universal hashing#Hashing strings|string hashing function]] ''djb2''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cse.yorku.ca/~oz/hash.html|title=String hash functions|last=Yigit|first=Ozan}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://groups.google.com/g/comp.lang.c/c/lSKWXiuNOAk/m/zstZ3SRhCjgJ|title=Hash function constants selection discussion}}</ref> and the [[cdb (software)|cdb]] database library.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cr.yp.to/cdb.html|title=cdb}}</ref>

== Mathematics ==
Bernstein has published a number of papers on [[mathematics]] and [[computation]]. Many of his papers deal with [[algorithm]]s or implementations.

In 2001, Bernstein circulated "Circuits for [[integer factorization]]: a proposal,"<ref>{{cite web | url = https://cr.yp.to/papers.html#nfscircuit | author = Daniel J. Bernstein | title = Circuits for integer factorization: a proposal |website=cr.yp.to | date = 2001-11-09}}</ref> which suggested that, if physical hardware implementations could be brought close to their theoretical efficiency, the then-popular estimates of adequate security parameters might be off by a factor of three. Since 512-bit [[RSA (algorithm)|RSA]] was breakable at the time, so might be 1536-bit RSA. Bernstein was careful not to make any actual predictions, and emphasized the importance of correctly interpreting [[Asymptotic analysis|asymptotic]] expressions. Several prominent researchers (among them [[Arjen Lenstra]], [[Adi Shamir]], Jim Tomlinson, and [[Eran Tromer]]) disagreed strongly with Bernstein's conclusions.<ref>{{cite journal | url = <!-- http://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~tromer/papers/meshc/meshc.html redirects to --> https://cs-people.bu.edu/tromer/papers/meshc/meshc.html |author1=Arjen K. Lenstra |author-link1=Arjen Lenstra |author2=Adi Shamir |author-link2=Adi Shamir |author3=Jim Tomlinson |author4=Eran Tromer |author-link4=Eran Tromer | title = Analysis of Bernstein's Factorization Circuit | journal = Proc. Asiacrypt | year = 2002 | volume = LNCS 2501 | pages = 1–26}}</ref>

Bernstein is also the author of the mathematical [[Library (computing)|libraries]] DJBFFT, a fast [[Software portability|portable]] [[Fast Fourier transform|FFT]] library, and <code>primegen</code>, an asymptotically fast small prime [[Sieve theory|sieve]] with low [[memory footprint]] based on the [[sieve of Atkin]] (rather than the more usual [[sieve of Eratosthenes]]). ''Sieve of Atkin'' was co-authored by Atkin and Bernstein. Both have been used effectively in the search for large [[prime number]]s.

In 2007, Bernstein proposed the use of a [[Twisted Edwards curve|(twisted) Edwards curve]], [[Curve25519]], as a basis for [[elliptic curve cryptography]]; it is employed in Ed25519 implementation of [[EdDSA]].

In February 2015, Bernstein and others published a paper on a stateless [[Post-quantum cryptography|post-quantum]] [[Hash-based cryptography|hash-based signature scheme]] called [[SPHINCS]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=SPHINCS: practical stateless hash-based signatures |url=https://sphincs.cr.yp.to/ |access-date=December 25, 2024 |website=sphincs.cr.yp.to}}</ref> In July 2022, [[SPHINCS+]], a signature scheme adapted from SPHINCS by Bernstein and others, was one of four algorithms selected as winners of the [[NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization]] competition. It was the only hash-based algorithm of the four winners.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2022-07-05 |title=NIST Announces First Four Quantum-Resistant Cryptographic Algorithms |url=https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2022/07/nist-announces-first-four-quantum-resistant-cryptographic-algorithms |journal=NIST |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Computer Security Division |first=Information Technology Laboratory |date=2017-01-03 |title=Selected Algorithms 2022 - Post-Quantum Cryptography {{!}} CSRC {{!}} CSRC |url=https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/post-quantum-cryptography/selected-algorithms-2022 |access-date=2024-03-27 |website=CSRC {{!}} NIST |language=EN-US}}</ref>

In April 2017, Bernstein and others published a paper on Post-Quantum RSA that includes an integer factorization algorithm claimed to be "often much faster than [[Shor's algorithm|Shor's]]".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Post-quantam RSA |url=https://cr.yp.to/papers/pqrsa-20170419.pdf |access-date=June 11, 2024 |website=cr.yp.to}}</ref>

== Teaching ==
In 2004, Bernstein taught a course on [[Application security|computer software security]] where he assigned each student to find ten [[Vulnerability (computing)|vulnerabilities]] in published software.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnet.com/news/students-uncover-dozens-of-unix-software-flaws/|title=Students uncover dozens of Unix software flaws|last=Lemos|first=Robert|date=2004-12-16|website=CNET|language=en|access-date=2019-03-21}}</ref> The 25 students discovered 44 vulnerabilities, and the class published [[Vulnerability (computing)|security advisories]] about the issues.<ref name=":0" />
